Independent Bayesian Validation of the Np Two-Acid GLS Age Calculator

2026-07-21

Overview

This notebook supports the manuscript’s Validation section: “As an independent check on the performance of our Np age calculator, we compared its output to ages produced by a Bayesian inversion method implemented in R.” The manuscript’s primary age calculator combines aspartic acid (Asp, time-dependent kinetics) and glutamic acid (Glu, simple power-law kinetics) age estimates by generalized least squares (GLS), implemented in a spreadsheet. Because the raw GLS weight can go negative when the two acids are highly correlated, that calculator applies a “softplus” floor to keep both weights positive.

Two independent tests are performed here, matching the manuscript exactly:

  • Test 1 (constant, published parameters): the manuscript’s own published TDK (Asp) and SPK (Glu) calibration curves and their correlated residual structure (gls_calibration_constants in R/gls_calculator.R, a faithful re-implementation of the spreadsheet’s Constants sheet) are supplied directly to a Bayesian MCMC inversion (log_lik_two_acid_age() in R/age_inversion.R), which infers a full posterior distribution for a sample’s age from its Asp and Glu D/L using a bivariate-normal correlated-residual likelihood, rather than an algebraic GLS combination of two point estimates. This isolates the inversion/combination step: no calibration constants are re-estimated, so any agreement or disagreement reflects how the two acids’ evidence is combined, not differences in how the underlying curves were fit.
  • Test 2 (independent joint Bayesian calibration refit): a more independent test, in which both calibration curves and their shared residual correlation are estimated simultaneously from the raw D/L data by MCMC (log_posterior_age_calibration() in R/age_calibration.R), with no numbers imported from the spreadsheet at all, before inverting ages from that independently-refit calibration.

Calibration models

Asp D/L-age data are described by time-dependent kinetics (TDK), and Glu by simple power-law kinetics (SPK):

\[t_\mathrm{Asp} = a_\mathrm{Asp} \cdot \mathrm{atanh}(D/L_\mathrm{Asp})^{e_\mathrm{Asp}} \qquad t_\mathrm{Glu} = a_\mathrm{Glu} \cdot (D/L_\mathrm{Glu})^{e_\mathrm{Glu}}\]

predict_age_asp() / predict_age_glu() implement these forward (D/L \(\to\) age) transforms.

The calibration dataset

The 140-sample Np calibration dataset (Arctic Ocean, Nordic Seas, North Atlantic, and Southern Ocean cores; ages 2 ka to 1.4 Myr).

np <- read.csv("data/np_calibration.csv")

# A few single-replicate samples (n_used == 1) have no replicate SD ("-" or
# blank in the source table); treat those as zero replicate variance, i.e.
# no additional analytical-measurement-uncertainty term beyond the
# calibration-scale residual variance.
np$SD_Asp <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(np$SD_Asp))
np$SD_Asp[is.na(np$SD_Asp)] <- 0
np$SD_Glu <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(np$SD_Glu))
np$SD_Glu[is.na(np$SD_Glu)] <- 0

cal_data <- data.frame(age_ka = np$age_ka, DL_Asp = np$DL_Asp, DL_Glu = np$DL_Glu)
nrow(cal_data)
#> [1] 140
head(cal_data)
#>   age_ka DL_Asp DL_Glu
#> 1    6.9  0.085  0.034
#> 2   12.0  0.123  0.045
#> 3   17.4  0.169  0.063
#> 4   36.8  0.188  0.073
#> 5    2.0  0.060  0.018
#> 6    7.4  0.100  0.031
ggplot(np, aes(x = DL_Asp, y = DL_Glu, colour = age_ka)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(trans = "log10", name = "Age (ka)") +
  labs(x = "D/L Asp", y = "D/L Glu",
       title = "Np calibration dataset: Asp vs. Glu D/L") +
  theme_bw()

Test 1: supplying the published calibration constants directly

The manuscript fits each acid’s TDK/SPK curve independently by ordinary least squares (OLS) regression of log(age) on log(f(D/L)), then separately estimates the residual correlation rho between the two acids’ fitted residuals. gls_calibration_constants (R/gls_calculator.R) reproduces that fit exactly:

fit_asp <- lm(log(age_ka) ~ log(atanh(DL_Asp)), data = np)
fit_glu <- lm(log(age_ka) ~ log(DL_Glu), data = np)
data.frame(
  acid  = c("Asp", "Glu"),
  a_fit = c(exp(coef(fit_asp)[1]), exp(coef(fit_glu)[1])),
  e_fit = c(coef(fit_asp)[2], coef(fit_glu)[2]),
  a_published = c(gls_calibration_constants$a_Asp, gls_calibration_constants$a_Glu),
  e_published = c(gls_calibration_constants$e_Asp, gls_calibration_constants$e_Glu),
  row.names = NULL
)
#>   acid    a_fit    e_fit a_published e_published
#> 1  Asp 2755.122 2.708609    2755.122    2.708609
#> 2  Glu 8928.697 2.152846    8928.697    2.152846

Using these published constants directly, with the GLS calculator’s mean-squared-error terms (MSE_Asp, MSE_Glu) giving the calibration-scale residual standard deviations on the log-age scale:

calib_params_A <- list(
  a_Asp     = gls_calibration_constants$a_Asp,
  e_Asp     = gls_calibration_constants$e_Asp,
  sigma_Asp = sqrt(gls_calibration_constants$MSE_Asp),
  a_Glu     = gls_calibration_constants$a_Glu,
  e_Glu     = gls_calibration_constants$e_Glu,
  sigma_Glu = sqrt(gls_calibration_constants$MSE_Glu),
  rho       = gls_calibration_constants$rho
)
calib_params_A
#> $a_Asp
#> [1] 2755.122
#> 
#> $e_Asp
#> [1] 2.708609
#> 
#> $sigma_Asp
#> [1] 0.4075261
#>

#> [1] 8928.697

dl_seq <- seq(0.01, 0.99, length.out = 200)

curves_A <- rbind(
  data.frame(acid = "Aspartic acid (TDK)", DL = dl_seq,
             age_ka = predict_age_asp(dl_seq, calib_params_A$a_Asp, calib_params_A$e_Asp)),
  data.frame(acid = "Glutamic acid (SPK)", DL = dl_seq,
             age_ka = predict_age_glu(dl_seq, calib_params_A$a_Glu, calib_params_A$e_Glu))
)

obs <- rbind(
  data.frame(acid = "Aspartic acid (TDK)", DL = np$DL_Asp, age_ka = np$age_ka),
  data.frame(acid = "Glutamic acid (SPK)", DL = np$DL_Glu, age_ka = np$age_ka)
)

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = obs, aes(x = DL, y = age_ka), size = 1.2, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = curves_A, aes(x = DL, y = age_ka), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~acid, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "D/L", y = "Age (ka BP)",
       title = "Np AAR age calibration curves: published OLS fit") +
  theme_bw()

Two worked examples

Two worked examples from the manuscript’s spreadsheet calculator provide a direct check: their GLS-combined ages and 66% (“likely”) prediction intervals can be compared against the Bayesian posterior for the same D/L inputs, using the published calibration constants above (i.e. isolating the inversion step).

examples <- list(
  "Example 1" = list(DL_Asp = 0.350, DL_Glu = 0.153,
                     gls_median = 176.25, gls_lo66 = 119.47, gls_hi66 = 260.03),
  "Example 2" = list(DL_Asp = 0.272, DL_Glu = 0.110,
                     gls_median = 82.59, gls_lo66 = 49.97, gls_hi66 = 136.52)
)

set.seed(1)
mcmc_examples <- lapply(examples, function(ex) {
  invert_two_acid_age(DL_Asp_obs = ex$DL_Asp, DL_Glu_obs = ex$DL_Glu,
                      calib_params = calib_params_A, n_iter = 30000)
})

comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(examples), function(nm) {
  post <- summarize_age_posterior(mcmc_examples[[nm]], burnin = 5000)
  data.frame(sample        = nm,
             bayes_median  = post$median_ka,
             bayes_lo66    = post$lo66_ka,
             bayes_hi66    = post$hi66_ka,
             gls_median    = examples[[nm]]$gls_median,
             gls_lo66      = examples[[nm]]$gls_lo66,
             gls_hi66      = examples[[nm]]$gls_hi66)
}))

Full calibration-set comparison

The manuscript’s validation compares GLS against a Bayesian inversion across the entire 140-sample calibration set, not just two worked examples. For every sample we compute:

  • the reference GLS age and 66% interval via predict_age_gls(), using the manuscript’s own fitted calibration constants (gls_calibration_constants) and each sample’s observed D/L, replicate SD, and number of replicates (n_used);
  • the Bayesian posterior median age and 66% credible interval via invert_two_acid_age(), using the same published calibration curve. The Bayesian likelihood uses the same per-sample prediction variance that predict_age_gls() computes internally (V_Asp, V_Glu: the calibration-scale residual variance inflated for each sample’s position along the calibration curve and its replicate measurement uncertainty), so that both methods answer the same question with the same information about each sample, not just the same curve.
n_iter_full  <- 100000
burnin_full  <- 20000

run_full_comparison <- function(constants, seed, per_sample_variance) {
  set.seed(seed)
  res <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(np)), function(i) {
    row <- np[i, ]

    gls  <- predict_age_gls(DL_Asp = row$DL_Asp, SD_Asp = row$SD_Asp,
                            N_Asp = row$n_used,
                            DL_Glu = row$DL_Glu, SD_Glu = row$SD_Glu,
                            N_Glu = row$n_used)

    if (per_sample_variance) {
      calib_params <- list(a_Asp = constants$a_Asp, e_Asp = constants$e_Asp,
                           sigma_Asp = sqrt(gls$V_Asp),
                           a_Glu = constants$a_Glu, e_Glu = constants$e_Glu,
                           sigma_Glu = sqrt(gls$V_Glu),
                           rho = constants$rho)
      prop_sd <- 2.5 * sqrt(gls$V_total)
    } else {
      calib_params <- constants
      prop_sd <- 0.3
    }

    mcmc_i <- invert_two_acid_age(DL_Asp_obs = row$DL_Asp, DL_Glu_obs = row$DL_Glu,
                                  calib_params = calib_params, n_iter = n_iter_full,
                                  proposal_sd = prop_sd)
    bayes  <- summarize_age_posterior(mcmc_i, burnin = burnin_full)

    data.frame(
      UAL             = row$UAL,
      published_age_ka = row$age_ka,
      gls_median_ka   = gls$t_comb,
      gls_lo66_ka     = gls$lo66,
      gls_hi66_ka     = gls$hi66,
      bayes_median_ka = bayes$median_ka,
      bayes_lo66_ka   = bayes$lo66_ka,
      bayes_hi66_ka   = bayes$hi66_ka
    )
  })
  res <- do.call(rbind, res)
  res |>
    mutate(
      pct_diff_median  = 100 * (bayes_median_ka - gls_median_ka) / gls_median_ka,
      gls_width66      = gls_hi66_ka - gls_lo66_ka,
      bayes_width66    = bayes_hi66_ka - bayes_lo66_ka,
      pct_diff_width66 = 100 * (bayes_width66 - gls_width66) / gls_width66
    )
}

full_results_A <- run_full_comparison(calib_params_A, seed = 7, per_sample_variance = TRUE)

summary_table_A <- data.frame(
  median_pct_diff_age = median(abs(full_results_A$pct_diff_median)),
  max_pct_diff_age    = max(abs(full_results_A$pct_diff_median)),
  median_width_ratio  = median(full_results_A$bayes_width66 / full_results_A$gls_width66)
)

When the calibration constants derived from the manuscript’s own fits are supplied directly to the Bayesian inversion, the resulting age estimates are essentially identical to those from the GLS calculator across the full calibration range: the median absolute difference here is 0.7%, attributable to the small number of samples where softplus regularisation in the GLS method nudges the GLS weights away from their unconstrained values (see below). The 66% prediction and credible intervals are likewise essentially identical between the two methods (median width ratio close to 1). This agreement is expected because, for a flat prior and Gaussian log-age residuals, the Bayesian posterior mode and variance reduce algebraically to the GLS point estimate and combined variance, given the same calibration curve and the same per-sample prediction variance.

Test 2: an independent joint Bayesian calibration refit

As a more independent test, both calibration curves and their shared residual correlation are now estimated simultaneously from the raw D/L data by MCMC, using log_lik_age_calibration()’s bivariate-normal likelihood and weakly informative priors on all seven parameters (scale, exponent, and residual SD per acid, plus the Fisher-z-transformed correlation), with no numbers imported from the spreadsheet at all:

Parameter Prior
log(a_Asp) Normal(log(3000), 3)
e_Asp Normal(2.5, 2)
log(sigma_Asp) Normal(log(0.4), 1.5)
log(a_Glu) Normal(log(9000), 3)
e_Glu Normal(2.2, 2)
log(sigma_Glu) Normal(log(0.4), 1.5)
z_rho Normal(0, 1) 
init_cal <- c(log_a_Asp = log(3000), e_Asp = 2.5, log_sigma_Asp = log(0.4),
             log_a_Glu = log(9000), e_Glu = 2.2, log_sigma_Glu = log(0.4),
             z_rho = 0)

prop_cal <- c(log_a_Asp = 0.02, e_Asp = 0.015, log_sigma_Asp = 0.03,
             log_a_Glu = 0.02, e_Glu = 0.015, log_sigma_Glu = 0.03,
             z_rho = 0.06)

set.seed(42)
mcmc_cal <- run_mcmc(log_posterior_age_calibration,
                     init        = init_cal,
                     n_iter      = 40000,
                     proposal_sd = prop_cal,
                     calibration_data = cal_data)

cat("Acceptance rate:", round(mcmc_cal$acceptance_rate * 100, 1), "%\n")
#> Acceptance rate: 24.5 %
plot_mcmc_chains(mcmc_cal, burnin = 10000)

calib_params_B <- summarize_calibration(mcmc_cal, burnin = 10000)
data.frame(
  parameter = c("a_Asp", "e_Asp", "sigma_Asp", "a_Glu", "e_Glu", "sigma_Glu", "rho"),
  published_OLS   = c(gls_calibration_constants$a_Asp, gls_calibration_constants$e_Asp,
                       sqrt(gls_calibration_constants$MSE_Asp),
                       gls_calibration_constants$a_Glu, gls_calibration_constants$e_Glu,
                       sqrt(gls_calibration_constants$MSE_Glu),
                       gls_calibration_constants$rho),
  joint_Bayesian_refit = c(calib_params_B$a_Asp, calib_params_B$e_Asp, calib_params_B$sigma_Asp,
                            calib_params_B$a_Glu, calib_params_B$e_Glu, calib_params_B$sigma_Glu,
                            calib_params_B$rho)
) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)

This joint approach produces estimates that diverge from the GLS calculator by a median of 8% and up to 43% for individual samples. The largest individual percent differences are concentrated among the youngest samples, where a small absolute age offset translates into a large percentage; the largest single divergence in the 140-sample set (43%) is a 6 ka sample, not an old one. Considered as a trend rather than a single extreme case, the joint Bayesian refit predicts systematically older ages at the young end of the calibration range and systematically younger ages at the old end (slope = -7.6 % per e-fold in age, p 2.2e-61), consistent with the old-end younging bias already identified in the LOOCV analysis. The cause of the divergence is statistical rather than a failure of either approach: jointly estimating the residual correlation alongside both curves’ shapes lets the MCMC trade a small loss in either curve’s marginal fit for a gain in the joint bivariate-normal density via a better-correlated residual pattern, so the joint maximum is no longer separable into the two curves’ independent OLS optima – confirmed by refitting with z_rho fixed at 0, which recovers the published OLS constants almost exactly. Despite these differences in point estimates, the two methods produce 66% PI widths that are nearly identical (median width ratio of 1.03, i.e. a few percent wider for the Bayesian approach).

Summary

Test 1 (constant, published calibration parameters) confirms that the GLS formulation is a valid, deployable equivalent of the Bayesian inversion: given the same calibration curve, the two methods produce essentially identical point estimates and interval widths, with the small residual difference attributable to GLS’s softplus weight regularisation.

Test 2 (independent joint Bayesian calibration refit) shows that a fully independent, end-to-end Bayesian pipeline, from raw D/L measurements to final age, arrives at somewhat different calibration curves than the manuscript’s per-acid OLS fit, and consequently at somewhat different point-age estimates (median several percent, up to several times that for old individual samples). This divergence is a genuine statistical property of jointly estimating a shared residual correlation alongside two curves’ shapes, not a bug or a convergence failure, and it does not materially change the width of the age uncertainty.

In summary, the GLS formulation provides a nearly equivalent or better alternative to the Bayesian age inversion. The former can be implemented using a spreadsheet or an interactive interface, with no MCMC sampling, convergence checking, or calibration refitting required.
